items.title: A note in a margin that took 358 years to verify
items.claim: Pierre de Fermat wrote in 1637 that he had a proof — too long for the margin — that a to the n + b to the n equals c to the n has no positive-integer solutions for n greater than 2. Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.
items.prompt: Why was Fermat's Last Theorem so hard to prove?

options.text: Fermat lied about having a proof — there isn't one

It was eventually shown to be equivalent to a statement about modular forms and elliptic curves (the Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture); the modern proof required machinery that didn't exist until the 1980s
Number theorists weren't trying hard enough
It is undecidable in standard axioms

items.reveal_title: Wiles, Frey, Ribet — a chain of insights
items.reveal:
Fermat wrote his marginal note in Diophantus's Arithmetica. Hundreds of mathematicians attempted the proof. Special cases were handled (n = 4 by Fermat himself; n = 3 by Euler; n = 5, 7 in the 1800s).

In 1985, Frey proposed that any non-trivial solution would correspond to an unusual elliptic curve. In 1986, Ribet proved this curve could not be 'modular'. Combined with the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture (all elliptic curves are modular), no solution could exist.

Wiles worked in secret for seven years on Taniyama-Shimura for a key class of elliptic curves. He announced the proof in 1993. A gap was found. With Richard Taylor he repaired it in late 1994. The proof runs over 100 pages and uses 20th-century algebraic geometry that Fermat couldn't have had.

It's almost certain Fermat did not have a real proof. He probably had a flawed attempt for small cases, since he never mentioned the result in subsequent letters.
items.why: Fermat's Last Theorem feels like an elementary statement about integers. Its proof needed centuries of machinery — number theory, algebraic geometry, automorphic forms — that no one in 1637 could have imagined.

items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.

items.title: The first theorem proved by computer
items.claim: Conjectured in 1852: any map can be coloured with 4 colours so no neighbouring regions share a colour. Proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 — using 1200 hours of computer time and case-by-case verification. Mathematicians argued for years about whether it counted.
items.prompt: Why was the computer proof controversial?

options.text: Computers were not allowed to do mathematics
The proof reduced the problem to 1936 'unavoidable configurations' and checked each by computer; no human could read the entire proof, and verification depended on trusting the computer code
The proof contained a subtle error

items.reveal:
The four-colour theorem was first conjectured by Francis Guthrie in 1852. Numerous false proofs were published (including Kempe's 1879 'proof', which stood for 11 years before Heawood found the gap).

Appel and Haken (University of Illinois) reduced the problem to checking that 1936 configurations were 'reducible'. A computer ran the checks over 1200 hours.

Mathematicians' objections: a proof is supposed to be readable, checkable and persuasive to humans. This one wasn't.

Follow-up proofs simplified the configurations (Robertson, Sanders, Seymour, Thomas, 1996: 633 cases) and have been formally verified by proof assistants (Gonthier, 2005, using Coq). Most mathematicians now accept the theorem, though some retain reservations about computer-assisted proofs in general.

It set the template for many later computer-assisted proofs: the Kepler conjecture (Hales, 2014), the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem (200 terabytes of evidence).
items.why: Proof is imagined as a human activity. Computer-assisted proof is a hybrid form that still divides mathematical philosophy — what is a proof, who certifies it, who is it for?
